items.stem: Tomás is planning a study of the importance of social class to people’s sense of identity. Explain one limitation of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: They are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the importance of social class to people’s sense of identity. [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “What is seen as deviant can change over time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. For example, attitudes to cohabitation, tattoos and same-sex relationships have changed in many societies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating long-term trends in divorce. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying long-term trends in divorce but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the effect of teachers’ expectations on pupils’ progress. Explain two strengths of using unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. Rapport between interviewer and interviewee builds trust, so people may reveal more, producing valid data. 2. They produce rich, detailed qualitative data that gives verstehen (an empathetic understanding).
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the effect of teachers’ expectations on pupils’ progress. [4]

items.stem: Felix studies 15 pupils from one school in Karachi and claims that the findings apply to all pupils in the country. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: research should be reliable and representative so that findings can be generalised and tested; standardised, large-scale methods such as questionnaires achieve this.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Official statistics always give an accurate picture of society.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many (especially soft) statistics are shaped by reporting, recording and definitions, so they may be inaccurate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of children’s independent mobility (450 children aged 8-11, Lima). Table: percentage of children allowed to | 1990 | 2025. Walk to school alone | 69% | 29%. Play outside without an adult | 68% | 37%. Visit shops alone | 51% | 29%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Visit shops alone between 1990 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that childhood has become more controlled by adults.
items.answer: (a) (29 − 51) ÷ 51 × 100 = -43.1%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure fell for Walk to school alone, Play outside without an adult, Visit shops alone; Play outside without an adult had the highest figure for 2025. Parents have become more concerned about traffic and “stranger danger” (a culture of risk). Qualifications: Children have more rights and voice in many ways; online freedom has increased even as physical freedom has declined; experiences vary by class and area. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 450 children aged 8-11 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (29 − 51) ÷ 51 × 100; 1 mark for -43.1% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how first-generation university students experience class. Explain two limitations of using field experiments for this research.
items.answer: 1. Deceiving people about sensitive matters may cause harm or distress. 2. They are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how first-generation university students experience class. [4]

items.stem: In one society women do most farming while men care for children; in another society near Lisbon the roles are reversed. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: the self develops through interaction with others; lack of interaction means the self, language and the ability to take the role of the other cannot develop (Mead).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Triangulation means using three different methods.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It means using more than one method or source to check findings; it need not be three.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Assess how useful laboratory experiments are for studying the impact of advertising on family spending.
items.answer: Strengths: the researcher controls variables, so cause and effect relationships can be identified; results are quantitative and easy to compare. Limitations: only small samples can be studied, so results are difficult to generalise; the artificial setting means people may not behave as they would in real life, so validity is low. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the impact of advertising on family spending but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Sofia, a sociology student, is designing a project on workers’ attitudes towards their employers in a large factory. Explain two limitations of using semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. Interviewer bias may still affect answers. 2. Follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to workers’ attitudes towards their employers in a large factory. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Madrid wants to study a secretive religious group that refuses to talk to outsiders. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: sociology should study society scientifically, using quantitative, reliable methods such as questionnaires and official statistics to discover social facts, correlations and causes; the researcher should remain objective and detached (Comte, Durkheim).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Positive sanctions are punishments.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Positive sanctions are rewards for conforming; negative sanctions are punishments.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of unstructured interviews for studying the influence of social media on teenagers’ values.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; rapport between interviewer and interviewee builds trust, so people may reveal more, producing valid data. Limitations: they cannot measure patterns across a large population because only a few people can be interviewed; samples are small, so findings are difficult to generalise. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the influence of social media on teenagers’ values but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Zara uses official unemployment statistics to measure change in Riyadh over ten years, although the government changed the definition of “unemployed” during the period. Explain how an interpretivist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: official statistics are social constructions produced by the decisions of officials and the public, so they tell us more about those decisions than about the reality they claim to measure (Atkinson, Cicourel).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Parents in Muscat give their son toy cars and praise him for being “tough”, while they buy their daughter dolls and praise her for being “kind”. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: people now choose from a wide range of global cultural influences, especially through the media, so socialisation is more fragmented and identities are more fluid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Marxists believe that society is based on value consensus.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Marxism is a conflict theory: apparent agreement reflects ruling-class ideology, not genuine consensus.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics to research why some young people leave school early.
items.answer: Strengths: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect; they are collected regularly, so trends over time and comparisons between groups can be made. Limitations: they cannot tell us how people feel or why they act as they do; they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why some young people leave school early but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Amara and her partner have lived together in Kathmandu for eight years and have two children; they say marriage is “just a piece of paper”. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: the family is a patriarchal institution in which men benefit from women’s unpaid domestic and emotional labour and domestic violence maintains male control (Delphy and Leonard).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: In Accra, the average number of children per woman has fallen from 4.2 to 1.8 in forty years, while the number of people over 80 has doubled. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: whether, when and how many children to have is an individual lifestyle choice; life courses are increasingly diverse.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Unstructured interviews are easy to repeat, so they are highly reliable.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Each unstructured interview is unique, so they are difficult to replicate and less reliable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) to research the role of grandparents in childcare.
items.answer: Strengths: they show how people themselves understood their experiences; they are often cheap to obtain and produced without the researcher influencing them. Limitations: they cannot show how common a pattern is across a society; they may not be authentic or credible; the writer may exaggerate or present themselves favourably. Theory: personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the role of grandparents in childcare but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Mei is planning a study of family structure in the nineteenth century. Explain two limitations of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: 1. They are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. 2. They show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to family structure in the nineteenth century. [4]
